title: AI at the Trump-Xi summit + Taiwan + EV overcapacities
gist: MERICS China Essentials ahead of the Trump-Xi summit: pre-agreed tariff-truce extension to January 10 and a rare-earth export-control pause, but low odds of any AI grand bargain (maybe an AI crisis hotline); quiet mutual testing over Taiwan with regional allies filling gaps; a new EV five-year plan that nominally curbs overcapacity but likely won't; and new exit/entry rules weaponizing travel for supply-chain security. Plus data on PhD surge and China's 40% share of global container exports.

insights.claim: Ahead of the September 2026 Trump-Xi meeting, the US extended the suspension of additional tariffs under the 2025 Busan Agreement until January 10, and China agreed not to further tighten rare-earth export controls for now.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Near-term tariff and rare-earth supply risk is deferred, but only to a hard January 10 date.
insights.quote: The US extended the suspension of additional tariffs negotiated in the 2025 Busan Agreement until January 10; China will not further tighten export controls on rare earths for the time being.

insights.claim: Mutual distrust makes significant US-China AI accords unlikely; both sides will likely aim for small achievable results such as a US-proposed AI-specific crisis hotline.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Don't price any easing of AI chip export controls from the summit.
insights.quote: A grand bargain between the US and China on AI safety is highly unlikely.
insights.locator: A grand bargain between the US

insights.claim: Locked in a Cold War-like spiral of distrust, neither the US nor China has sufficient incentive to slow its own AI development.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Supports continued AI capex and compute-race dynamics on both sides.
insights.quote: neither has sufficient incentive to put the brakes on its own AI development

insights.claim: Biden-era attempts at a common AI approach failed because Beijing demanded Washington relax trade restrictions on technologies China lacks.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China links AI safety cooperation to export-control relief, a likely recurring negotiating demand.

insights.claim: Beijing views US government and corporate calls for an AI slowdown as an excuse to blunt China's AI advance, while Washington fears Beijing would not comply with a negotiated slowdown.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Verification problems make AI arms-control style deals structurally hard.

insights.claim: China may be more open to AI talks than under Biden: Xi warned publicly in July 2026 for the first time about 'technological loss of control' in AI, China's security chief listed AI risks in September, and China's top AI standards body released version 3.0 of its safety framework.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese elite rhetoric on AI risk is shifting, opening a narrow channel for safety cooperation.
insights.quote: In July, Xi publicly warned for the first time about the risk of “technological loss of control” in AI

insights.claim: Despite new frameworks, safety guardrails for China's own AI industry are still lacking.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for Chinese AI firms could rise if Beijing moves from frameworks to enforcement.
insights.quote: Still, safety guardrails for China’s own AI industry are still lacking.

insights.claim: China's PhD graduates grew 110% in a decade, from about 54,000 in 2015 to almost 113,000 in 2025, while PhD admissions rose from about 74,000 to over 201,000.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Signals a fast-growing high-end talent pipeline supporting China's tech catch-up.

insights.claim: China still has only 62 doctoral graduates per million people, about a quarter of the US (240) and Europe (230) rates, but is likely to keep closing the gap.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Relative talent scale gap persists but is narrowing.
insights.quote: China still counts only 62 doctoral graduates per million people, one quarter of the rate of the US and Europe

insights.claim: Academic and professional opportunities for Chinese PhDs are failing to keep pace with graduate numbers; Shenzhen Middle School employs over 100 PhD-holding teachers, about a quarter of central-campus staff.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Credential oversupply points to graduate underemployment and talent misallocation in China.
insights.quote: Academic and professional opportunities for PhDs are already failing to keep pace with the number of graduates.

insights.claim: Since May 2025 the Trump administration has ordered only two US warship transits of the Taiwan Strait and effectively halted foreign military sales to Taiwan since Trump's China visit.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A material US pullback on Taiwan arms sales affects defense contractors and regional risk premia.

insights.claim: Beijing has refrained from major military exercises in the Taiwan Strait since its 29-31 December 2025 drills, which responded to Washington's last weapons sale to Taiwan.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Links Chinese drill escalation directly to US arms sales — a trigger to watch.

insights.claim: Regional actors are partly compensating for uncertain US security engagement with Taiwan: the Philippines may allow a second Taiwan office, New Zealand warships transited the Strait on 18 September, and Japan began deploying missiles able to strike Shanghai and Nanjing in March 2026.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Regional rearmament shifts Asia security risk away from a pure US-China axis and boosts allied defense demand.
insights.quote: other regional actors have partly compensated for growing uncertainty over US security engagement with Taiwan

insights.claim: This shift is potentially fraught for Taiwan given the strain Trump has placed on US alliances.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Fragmented security coverage could raise tail risk of miscalculation.

insights.claim: China's 15th Five-Year Plan for intelligent connected NEVs for the first time calls for managing auto production capacity via investment supervision of new projects, consolidation and stricter tech and safety standards.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Potential consolidation could favor leading Chinese EV makers over weaker players.
insights.locator: The plan for the first time

insights.claim: Local governments are likely to resist closing EV factories to avoid unemployment, stranded assets and losing the inter-regional race for the next EV champion, limiting overcapacity curbs.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Overcapacity and price pressure in global EV markets will likely persist.
insights.quote: Local governments are, in particular, likely to resist shuttering factories to avoid increasing unemployment

insights.claim: Despite overcapacity worries, the plan aims to entrench China's EV leadership and invites foreign firms to produce in China for export, so European firms should expect even more Chinese competition and Chinese firms will expand abroad.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Bearish for European automakers' margins and market share.
insights.quote: European companies and policymakers should expect even more competition from Chinese manufacturers.

insights.claim: China has suspended construction of new power and energy-storage battery projects pending a year-end capacity review.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Could tighten battery supply growth and constrain firms' expansion plans.
insights.quote: China has suspended construction of new power and energy-storage battery projects pending a year-end review.

insights.claim: China has added detailed cost-calculation rules for identifying below-cost selling, giving regulators a concrete basis to intervene in price wars.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Anti-involution enforcement could support margins in Chinese manufacturing sectors.

insights.claim: New Chinese exit-entry rules effective September 15, 2026 allow authorities to bar citizens with expertise in AI, engineering, advanced manufacturing or rare-earth processing from leaving.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Talent outflow controls deepen China's tech-protection regime and limit knowledge transfer.

insights.claim: Foreigners can be blocked from entering or leaving China if they or their employer are under investigation, on sanctions/countermeasure lists, or deemed a supply-chain security threat.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Executives of firms pursuing supply-chain diversification or due diligence face personal travel risk.
insights.quote: This means substantial new risks for international residents or visitors if they or their companies engage in supply chain diversification, due diligence

insights.claim: Visa-free entry and easier travel should not blind visitors to China's new travel-linked geopolitical risks.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Openness signals coexist with tightened coercive tools.

insights.claim: China accounted for 40% of global container exports over the past three months, a 2.5 percentage-point jump in nine months, showing trade imbalances growing faster than expected.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Rising Chinese export share raises odds of EU tariffs and trade friction.
insights.quote: China’s 40% share of global container exports over the past three months highlights its heavy reliance on trade to power economic growth.

insights.claim: Two former members of China's IPO review committee were convicted of bribery, one using a 'shadow shareholder' arrangement, receiving 9 and 10.5 year sentences.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Highlights governance risk in China's IPO approval process.

insights.claim: China's Supreme People's Court released rules for AI-related disputes covering civil liability, IP and contract violations.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Clarifies legal liability regime for AI firms operating in China.
